Eventual smoothness of generalized solutions to a singular chemotaxis-Stokes system

Tobias Black ††thanks: Institut für Mathematik, Universität Paderborn, Warburger Str. 100, 33098 Paderborn, Germany; Email address: tblack@math.upb.de
Abstract

Abstract: We study the chemotaxis-fluid system

{nt+u⋅∇n=Δn−∇⋅(nc∇c),x∈Ω,t>0,ct+u⋅∇c=Δ​c−n​c,x∈Ω,t>0,ut+∇P=Δu+n∇ϕ,x∈Ω,t>0,∇⋅u=0,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{r@{\,}c@{\,}c@{\ }l@{\quad}l@{\quad}l@{\,}c}n_{t}&+&u\cdot\!\nabla n&=\Delta n-\nabla\!\cdot(\frac{n}{c}\nabla c),&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ c_{t}&+&u\cdot\!\nabla c&=\Delta c-nc,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ u_{t}&+&\nabla P&=\Delta u+n\nabla\phi,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ &&\nabla\cdot u&=0,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\end{array}\right.

under homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions for nn and cc and homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions for uu, where Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is a bounded domain with smooth boundary and ϕ∈C2​(Ω¯)\phi\in C^{2}\left(\bar{\Omega}\right). From recent results it is known that for suitable regular initial data, the corresponding initial-boundary value problem possesses a global generalized solution. We will show that for small initial mass ∫Ωn0\int_{\Omega}\!n_{0} these generalized solutions will eventually become classical solutions of the system and obey certain asymptotic properties.

Moreover, from the analysis of certain energy-type inequalities arising during the investigation of the eventual regularity, we will also derive a result on global existence of classical solutions under assumption of certain smallness conditions on the size of n0n_{0} in L1​(Ω)L^{1}\!\left(\Omega\right) and in L​log⁡L​(Ω)L\log L\!\left(\Omega\right), u0u_{0} in L4​(Ω)L^{4}\!\left(\Omega\right), and of ∇c0\nabla c_{0} in L2​(Ω)L^{2}\!\left(\Omega\right).

Keywords: chemotaxis, Stokes, chemotaxis-fluid interaction, global existence, generalized solution, eventual regularity, stabilization

MSC (2010): 35B65, 35B40 (primary), 35K35, 35Q92, 92C17

1 Introduction

Even among the smallest and most primitive organisms there are cases of complex and macroscopical collective behavior, for instance bacteria of species E. coli were confirmed to form migrating bands when subjected to a test environment featuring gradients of nutrient concentration ([1]). Following these experimental findings, chemotaxis systems with singular sensitivity of the form

{nt=Δn−∇⋅(nc∇c),ct=Δ​c−n​c,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{r@{\,}l@{\quad}l}n_{t}&=\Delta n-\nabla\!\cdot(\frac{n}{c}\nabla c),\\ c_{t}&=\Delta c-nc,\\ \end{array}\right.

were among the first phenomenological models proposed by Keller and Segel ([12]) to study these processes of chemotactic migration. Herein, nn denotes the density of the bacteria which orient their movement towards increasing concentration cc of a chemical substance which serves as their food source and is thereby consumed in the process. Singular chemotactic sensitivities of the type featured in (1) express the system assumption that the signal is perceived as described by the Weber-Fechner law ([10],[23]). An outstanding facet of this system, as already illustrated in [12], is the occurence of wave-like solution behavior without any type of cell kinetics, which is known to be vital for such effects in standard reaction-diffusion equations. For studies on existence and stability properties of traveling wave solutions of (1) see [32, 17, 20] and references therein.

The results on global existence to systems of the form (1) are very sparse, with widely arbitrary initial data only being treated for the one-dimensional case ([28],[16]). In higher dimensions the results were constrained to the Cauchy problem for (1) in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with n∈{2,3}n\in\{2,3\}, where smallness conditions on the initial data had to be imposed to show the existence of globally defined classical solutions ([33]). Only recently ([38]), so called global generalized solutions to (1) were constructed in the two-dimensional case. The solutions are obtained through the study of a suitably chosen regularization guaranteeing that the regularized chemical concentration is strictly bounded away from zero for all times. These generalized solutions comply with the classical solution concept in the sense that generalized solutions which are sufficiently smooth also solve the system in the classical sense. In a sequel to the previously mentioned work the author furthermore proved that if the initial mass is small these generalized solutions eventually become classical solutions after some (possibly large) waiting time and that the solutions satisfy certain kind of asymptotic properties ([39]).
Eventual regularity and fluid interaction. Our interest slightly differing from the system proposed by Keller and Segel, where the model assumes no interaction between bacteria and surroundings, we will consider the case that the bacteria may be affected by their liquid environment. Here, we do not only assume that this interaction occurs by means of transport, but also in form of a feedback between the cells and the fluid velocity stemming from a buoyancy effect assumed in the model development featured in [29]. The experimental evidence reported in the latter reference suggests that the chemotactic motion inside the liquid can be substantially influenced by the feedback between cells and fluid, with turbulence emerging spontaneously in population of aerobic bacteria suspended in sessile drops of water. As a prototypical model for the description of this phenomenom a system of the form

{nt+u⋅∇n=Δn−∇⋅(n∇c),ct+u⋅∇c=Δ​c−n​c,ut+κ(u⋅∇)u=Δu+n∇ϕ−∇P∇⁣⋅⁡u=0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{r@{\,}c@{\,}c@{\,}l}n_{t}&+&u\cdot\!\nabla n&=\Delta n-\nabla\!\cdot(n\nabla c),\\ c_{t}&+&u\cdot\!\nabla c&=\Delta c-nc,\\ u_{t}&+&\kappa(u\cdot\nabla)u&=\Delta u+n\nabla\phi-\nabla P\\ &&\dive u&=0,\end{array}\right.

was proposed in [29] and has been the groundwork for many articles concerning the mathematical analysis of chemotaxis-fluid interaction since the first analytical results asserting local existence of weak solutions ([18]). Obtaining results concerning the global existence of solutions is far from trivial, even when u≡0u\equiv 0 the global existence of solutions is only known under a smallness condition on the initial data ([26]), or when N=2N=2 (e.g. [35]). These outcomes are similar in the case of u≢0u\not\equiv 0. In the two-dimensional setting global classical solutions stemming from reasonably smooth initial data have also been shown to exist in [35], whereas many results treating variants of (1) in three-dimensional frameworks are again restricted to weak solutions emanating from small initial data (e.g. [13],[4]). Nevertheless, even in theses cases, where global regularity is hard to prove, some results concerning eventual regularity of solutions have been shown. In particular, for the fluid free case eventual smoothness of solutions was shown in [27] for N=3N=3 and a result including fluid is contained in [40], where certain weak eventual energy solutions are considered.

Similar smoothing effects can also be observed in a setting where N=3N=3 and logistic growth terms of the form +ρ​n−μ​n2+\rho n-\mu n^{2} (ρ≥0,μ>0)(\rho\geq 0,\mu>0) are included in the first equation. In this framework it is still unclear whether global classical solutions exist for small μ>0\mu>0 and reasonably arbitrary initial data, but weak solutions which eventually become smooth are known to exist for any μ>0\mu>0 and possibly large initial data, as indicated by the studies in e.g. [15].

Chemotaxis-fluid system with singular sensitivity. In light of the regularizing effects observed in the chemotaxis and chemotaxis-fluid problems mentioned above it seems reasonable to assume that also in the case of singular sensitivity the smoothing effect of the second equation will eventually result in classical solutions even if fluid interaction with the bacteria is present. As the construction of weak solution used in [30] does not work for the full Navier-Stokes subsystem (as included in (1)) we instead work with the simpler Stokes realization of the fluid, which was also employed in [30], instead. In fact we will study systems of the form

{nt+u⋅∇n=Δn−∇⋅(nc∇c),x∈Ω,t>0,ct+u⋅∇c=Δ​c−n​c,x∈Ω,t>0,ut+∇P=Δu+n∇ϕ,x∈Ω,t>0,∇⁣⋅⁡u=0,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{r@{\,}c@{\,}c@{\,}l@{\quad}l@{\quad}l@{\,}c}n_{t}&+&u\cdot\!\nabla n&=\Delta n-\nabla\!\cdot(\frac{n}{c}\nabla c),&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ c_{t}&+&u\cdot\!\nabla c&=\Delta c-nc,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ u_{t}&+&\nabla P&=\Delta u+n\nabla\phi,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ &&\dive u&=0,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\end{array}\right.

with boundary conditions

∂n∂ν=∂c∂ν=0,andu=0for ​x∈∂Ω⁡ and ​t>0,\displaystyle\frac{\partial n}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial c}{\partial\nu}=0,\quad\text{and}\quad u=0\quad\text{for }x\in\romega\text{ and }t>0, (1.11)

and initial conditions

n⁡(x,0)=n0​(x),c⁡(x,0)=c0​(x),u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),x∈Ω.\displaystyle n(x,0)=n_{0}(x),\quad c(x,0)=c_{0}(x),\quad u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\quad x\in\Omega. (1.12)

Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} denotes a bounded domain with smooth boundary and the gravitational potential ϕ\phi is assumed to satisfy

ϕ∈C2​(Ω¯)withK1:=‖ϕ‖W1,∞​(Ω).\displaystyle\phi\in C^{2}\!\left(\bomega\right)\quad\text{with}\quad K_{1}:=\|\phi\|_{W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)}. (1.13)

For the initial distributions we will prescribe the regularity assumptions

{n0∈C0​(Ω¯)with ​n0≥0​ in ​Ω​ and ​n0≢0,c0∈W1,∞​(Ω)with ​c0>0​ in ​Ω¯,u0∈D⁡(Arα)for all ​r∈(1,∞)​ and some ​α∈(12,1),\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{r@{\,}l@{\quad}l}n_{0}&\in C^{0}\!\left(\bomega\right)&\text{with }n_{0}\geq 0\text{ in }\Omega\text{ and }n_{0}\not\equiv 0,\\ c_{0}&\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)&\text{with }c_{0}>0\text{ in }\bomega,\\ u_{0}&\in D\!\left(A^{\alpha}_{r}\right)&\text{for all }r\in(1,\infty)\text{ and some }\alpha\in(\frac{1}{2},1),\end{array}\right.

with ArA_{r} denoting the Stokes operator Ar:=−𝒫r​ΔA_{r}:=-\mathcal{P}_{r}\Delta in Lr​(Ω,ℝ2)L^{r\;\!}\!\left(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{2}\right) with domain D⁡(Ar)=W2,r​(Ω,ℝ2)∩W01,r​(Ω,ℝ2)∩Lσr​(Ω)D\left(A_{r}\right)=W^{2,r}\!\left(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)\cap W^{1,r}_{0}\!\left(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)\cap L^{r}_{\sigma}\!\left(\Omega\right), where Lσr​(Ω)={φ∈Lr​(Ω,ℝ2)|∇⁣⋅⁡φ=0}L^{r}_{\sigma}\!\left(\Omega\right)=\{\varphi\in L^{r\;\!}\!\left(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)\,|\,\dive\varphi=0\} stands for the solenodial subspace of Lr​(Ω,ℝ2)L^{r\;\!}\!\left(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{2}\right) obtained by the Helmholtz projection 𝒫r\mathcal{P}_{r}.

In this setting, building on the work [38], it was shown in [30] that for any (n0,c0,u0)(n_{0},c_{0},u_{0}) satisfying (1) the system (1) possesses at least on global generalized solution (in the sense of Definition 3.1 below). These solutions are constructed by a similar limiting procedure as in the fluid free setting, making sure that for each of the approximate solutions the quantity cc remains strictly positive throughout Ω\Omega for all times. In a simplified version the result on global existence of generalized solutions and basic decay properties of cc obtained in [30] can be summarized as follows.

Theorem A.


Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Then for all (n0,c0,u0)(n_{0},c_{0},u_{0}) satisfying (1), the problem (1)– (1.12) possesses at least one global generalized solution (n,c,u)(n,c,u) in the sense of Definition 3.1 below. For each p∈[1,∞)p\in[1,\infty) the solution has the properties that n⁡(⋅,t)∈Lp​(Ω)n(\cdot,t)\in L^{p}(\Omega) and ∇cc∈L2​(Ω)\frac{\nabla c}{c}\in L^{2}(\Omega) for a.e. t>0t>0. Moreover, cc is continuous on [0,∞)[0,\infty) as L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega)–valued function with respect to the weak–⋆\star topology on L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega), and satisfies

c⁡(⋅,t)​⇀⋆0in ​L∞​(Ω)andc⁡(⋅,t)→0in ​Lp​(Ω)as ​t→∞.\displaystyle c(\cdot,t)\wsto 0\quad\text{in }L^{\infty}(\Omega)\qquad\text{and}\qquad c(\cdot,t)\to 0\quad\text{in }L^{p}(\Omega)\qquad\text{as }t\to\infty.

Main results. The existence of global generalized solutions as provided by Theorem A at hand, it is the purpose of the present work to study the question how far the eventual regularity and stabilization results for small data, as obtained in [39] for (1), may be affected by the interaction of the bacteria with their liquid surroundings.

Theorem 1.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Then there exists some m⋆>0m_{\star}\!>0 such that for any (n0,c0,u0)(n_{0},c_{0},u_{0}) satisfying (1) as well as

∫Ωn0≤m⋆,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!n_{0}\leq m_{\star}, (1.17)

the global generalized solution of (1)– (1.12) from Theorem A has the property that there exists T>0T>0 such that

n∈C2,1(Ω¯×[T,∞)),c∈C2,1(Ω¯×[T,∞))andu∈C2,1(Ω¯×[T,∞);ℝ2),\displaystyle n\in C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times[T,\infty)\right),\quad c\in C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times[T,\infty)\right)\quad\text{and}\quad u\in C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times[T,\infty);\mathbb{R}^{2}\right), (1.18)

that

c⁡(x,t)>0for all ​x∈Ω¯⁡ and any ​t≥T,\displaystyle c(x,t)>0\quad\text{for all }x\in\bomega\text{ and any }t\geq T, (1.19)

and such that (n,c,u)(n,c,u) solve (1)– (1.12) classically in Ω×(T,∞)\Omega\times(T,\infty). Furthermore, this solution satisfies

n⁡(⋅,t)\displaystyle n(\cdot,t) →1|Ω|∫Ωn0in L∞(Ω),c(⋅,t)→0in L∞(Ω),u(⋅,t)→0in L∞(Ω),\displaystyle\to\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}\!n_{0}\quad\text{in }L^{\infty}(\Omega),\qquad c(\cdot,t)\to 0\quad\ \text{in }L^{\infty}(\Omega),\qquad u(\cdot,t)\to 0\quad\ \text{in }L^{\infty}(\Omega), (1.20)

and

∇c​(⋅,t)c⁡(⋅,t)→0in ​L∞​(Ω)\displaystyle\frac{\nabla c(\cdot,t)}{c(\cdot,t)}\to 0\quad\text{in }L^{\infty}(\Omega) (1.21)

as t→∞t\to\infty.

Our analysis will also in straightforward manner allow us to formulate a result for global classical solutions to (1)– (1.12) if certain smallness conditions are fulfilled by the initial distributions. Furthermore, these global classical solutions inherit the same asymptotic properties stated in Theorem 1.1. (1.23)

We obtain the following.

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Then there exists m⋆⁣⋆>0m_{\star\star}>0 such that for any (n0,c0,u0)(n_{0},c_{0},u_{0}) satisfying (1),

∫Ωn0≤m⋆⁣⋆,and∫Ω|u0|4≤m⋆⁣⋆\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!n_{0}\leq m_{\star\star},\quad\text{and}\quad\int_{\Omega}\!|u_{0}|^{4}\leq m_{\star\star} (1.24)

Notation. Throughout the article, in addition to the previously mentioned assumptions in (1.13) and (1) for Ω\Omega, ϕ\phi, the initial data, the Stokes operator and its semigroup, we will make use of the following notations. λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0 will always denote the first positive eigenvalue of the Stokes operator in Ω\Omega with respect to homogeneous Dirichlet boundary data. Since Arα​φ,e−t​Ar​φA^{\alpha}_{r}\varphi,e^{-tA_{r}}\varphi and 𝒫r​ψ\mathcal{P}_{r}\psi are independent of r∈(1,∞)r\in(1,\infty) for φ∈C0∞​(Ω)∩Lσr​(Ω)\varphi\in C_{0}^{\infty}\!\left(\Omega\right)\cap L_{\sigma}^{r}\!\left(\Omega\right) and ψ∈C0∞​(Ω)\psi\in C_{0}^{\infty}\!\left(\Omega\right), we will drop the subscript whenever there is no danger of confusion. Similar to denoting by Lσr​(Ω)L_{\sigma}^{r}\!\left(\Omega\right) all divergence free functions of Lp​(Ω)L^{p}(\Omega), the space of divergence free, smooth test functions with compact support in Ω×(0,∞)\Omega\times(0,\infty) will be denoted by C0,σ∞​(Ω×(0,∞))C^{\infty}_{0,\sigma}\!\left(\Omega\times(0,\infty)\right). Additionally, when talking about classical solutions to some of the featured systems in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) for some t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0, we will often shorten the notation to (n,c,u)∈C0​(Ω×[t0,∞))(n,c,u)\in C^{0}\!\left(\Omega\times[t_{0},\infty)\right), when we are actually considering (n,c,u,P)∈C0​(Ω×[t0,∞))×C0​(Ω×[t0,∞))×C0​(Ω×[t0,∞),ℝ2)×C1,0​(Ω¯×[t0,∞))(n,c,u,P)\in C^{0}\!\left(\Omega\times[t_{0},\infty)\right)\times C^{0}\!\left(\Omega\times[t_{0},\infty)\right)\times C^{0}\!\left(\Omega\times[t_{0},\infty);\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)\times C^{1,0}\!\left(\bomega\times[t_{0},\infty)\right). The notation (n,c,u)∈C2,1​(Ω×(t0,∞))(n,c,u)\in C^{2,1}\!\left(\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty)\right) will be used in a similar fashion.

2 Basic properties of a family of generalized problems

The construction of the generalized solution mentioned above is based on a limit procedure of solutions to regularized problems and a transformation thereof. Since the original problem (1) and the family of approximate problems in question are quite similar, we will first consider the even more general family of problems

{nt+u⋅∇n=Δn−∇⋅(n​f′​(n)c∇c),x∈Ω,t>0ct+u⋅∇c=Δ​c−f⁡(n)​c,x∈Ω,t>0,ut+∇P=Δu+n∇ϕ,x∈Ω,t>0,∇⁣⋅⁡u=0,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{r@{\,}c@{\,}c@{\,}l@{\quad}l@{\quad}l@{\,}c}n_{t}&+&u\cdot\!\nabla n&=\Delta n-\nabla\!\cdot\Big(\frac{nf^{\prime}(n)}{c}\nabla c\Big),&x\in\Omega,&t>0\\ c_{t}&+&u\cdot\!\nabla c&=\Delta c-f(n)c,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ u_{t}&+&\nabla P&=\Delta u+n\nabla\phi,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ &&\dive u&=0,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\end{array}\right.

where we only require that the functions f∈C3​([0,∞))f\in C^{3}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) satisfy

f(0)=0 and 0≤f′≤1 on [0,∞).\displaystyle f(0)=0\quad\text{ and }\quad 0\leq f^{\prime}\leq 1\text{ on }[0,\infty). (2.5)

Upon proper choice of a subfamily of these functions (c.f. (3.7) below) the system will be regularized in a way that ensures that cc is bounded away from zero, from which one can easily obtain global and bounded solutions to the corresponding approximate problems. These global and bounded solutions are one of the main ingredients of the limit process involved in the construction of the generalized solution ([38],[30]).

The problems (2) will be regarded under the boundary conditions

∂n∂ν=∂c∂ν=0,andu=0for ​x∈∂Ω⁡ and ​t∈(0,Tmax),\displaystyle\frac{\partial n}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial c}{\partial\nu}=0,\quad\text{and}\quad u=0\quad\text{for }x\in\romega\text{ and }t\in(0,T_{max}), (2.6)

and the initial conditions

n⁡(x,0)=n0​(x),c⁡(x,0)=c0​(x),u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),x∈Ω.\displaystyle n(x,0)=n_{0}(x),\quad c(x,0)=c_{0}(x),\quad u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\quad x\in\Omega. (2.7)

For any f∈C3​([0,∞))f\in C^{3}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) satisfying the conditions above, local existence of classical solutions can be obtained by well-established fixed point methods. Since the necessary adaptions are quite straightforward, we will refer to local existence proofs in closely related situations for details.

Lemma 2.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a bounded domain with smooth boundary, ϑ>2\vartheta>2 and f∈C3​([0,∞))f\in C^{3}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) satisfies (2.5). Then for all (n0,c0,u0)(n_{0},c_{0},u_{0}) satisfying (1) there exist Tm​a​x∈(0,∞]T_{max}\in(0,\infty] and uniquely determined functions

n\displaystyle n ∈C0​(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax)),\displaystyle\in C^{0}\!\left(\bomega\times[0,T_{max})\right)\cap C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times(0,T_{max})\right),

Tm​a​x=∞,\displaystyle\quad T_{max}=\infty,\, or ​lim inft↗Tm​a​xinfx∈Ωc⁡(x,t)=0,\displaystyle\mbox{ or }\,\liminf_{t\nearrow T_{max}}\inf_{x\in\Omega}c(x,t)=0, (2.8)
or ​lim supt↗Tm​a​x(‖n⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖c⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,ϑ​(Ω)+‖Aα​u​(⋅,t)‖L2​(Ω))=∞.\displaystyle\mbox{ or }\,\limsup_{t\nearrow T_{max}}\left(\|n(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|c(\cdot,t)\|_{W^{1,\vartheta}(\Omega)}+\|A^{\alpha}u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\right)=\infty.

Local existence, uniqueness and the blow-up criterion (2.8) can be obtained by straightforward adaption of well known arguments as detailed in [11, 6] and [35] for related situations. 2.1 Regularity of the Stokes subsystem

It is well known that the Stokes subsystem dd⁡tu+Au=𝒫(n∇ϕ)\frac{\intd}{\intd t}u+Au=\mathcal{P}(n\nabla\phi) in (3) has the property that the regularity of the spatial derivative ∇u\nabla u is solely reliant on the regularity of nn (since ∇ϕ\nabla\phi is bounded). In fact for Stokes systems of the form

{ut=Δu−∇P+n∇ϕ,x∈Ω,t0>0,∇⁣⋅⁡u=0,x∈Ω,t0>0,u=0,x∈∂Ω,t0>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{r@{\,}l@{\quad}l@{\quad}l@{\,}c}u_{t}&=\Delta u-\nabla P+n\nabla\phi,&x\in\Omega,&t_{0}>0,\\ \dive u&=0,&x\in\Omega,&t_{0}>0,\\ u&=0,&x\in\romega,&t_{0}>0,\end{array}\right.

we can obtain the following two results. The first is a refinement of a basic boundedness result e.g. featured in [31, Lemma 2.4].

Let ϕ∈C2​(Ω¯)\phi\in C^{2}\!\left(\bomega\right). There exist constants λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0 and Ku>0K_{u}>0 such that whenever u∈C0​(Ω¯×[t0,T0),ℝ2)∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(t0,T0),ℝ2)u\in C^{0}\!\left(\bomega\times[t_{0},T_{0});\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)\cap C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times(t_{0},T_{0});\mathbb{R}^{2}\right) is a classical solution of (2.1) in Ω×(t0,T0)\Omega\times(t_{0},T_{0}) for some 0≤t0<T0≤∞0\leq t_{0}<T_{0}\leq\infty and n∈C0​(Ω¯×[t0,T0))n\in C^{0}\!\left(\bomega\times[t_{0},T_{0})\right) satisfying

By the variation-of-constants representation for uu we have

u(⋅,t)=e−(t−t0)​Au(⋅,t0)+∫t0te−(t−s)​A𝒫(n(⋅,s)∇ϕ)dsfor all t∈(t0,T0).\displaystyle u(\cdot,t)=e^{-(t-t_{0})A}u(\cdot,t_{0})+\int_{t_{0}}^{t}e^{-(t-s)A}\mathcal{P}(n(\cdot,s)\nabla\phi)\intd s\quad\text{for all }t\in(t_{0},T_{0}).

Lemma 2.3.

In particular, in view of the mass conservation property of nn and the Sobolev embedding theorem, we can easily obtain bounds independent of ff for the quantity ‖u‖Lp​(Ω)\|u\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)} with p<∞p<\infty from the previous Lemma. For these potentially better bounds than the one provided by Lemma 2.2 however, we do not know the exact relation to u0u_{0}.

2.2 Logarithmic rescaling and basic a priori information on zz

Now, a quite standard change in variables transformation obtained by taking nn, cc and uu from Lemma 2.1 and setting

z:=−ln⁡(c‖c0‖L∞​(Ω)) and z0:=−ln⁡(c0‖c0‖L∞​(Ω)),\displaystyle z:=-\ln\left(\frac{c}{\|c_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}}\right)\quad\text{ and }\quad z_{0}:=-\ln\left(\frac{c_{0}}{\|c_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}}\right),

{nt+u⋅∇n=Δn+∇⋅(nf′(n)∇z),x∈Ω,t>0,zt−u⋅∇z=Δ​z−|∇z|2+f⁡(n),x∈Ω,t>0,ut+∇P=Δu+n∇ϕ,x∈Ω,t>0,∇⁣⋅⁡u=0,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{r@{\,}c@{\,}c@{\,}l@{\quad}l@{\quad}l@{\,}c}n_{t}&+&u\cdot\!\nabla n&=\Delta n+\nabla\!\cdot(nf^{\prime}(n)\nabla z),&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ z_{t}&-&u\cdot\!\nabla z&=\Delta z-|\nabla z|^{2}+f(n),&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ u_{t}&+&\nabla P&=\Delta u+n\nabla\phi,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ &&\dive u&=0,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\end{array}\right.

which build the basis for our analysis of the energy-type inequalities featured in Section 4.1. This transformation has been thoroughly used in previous literature (see e.g. [33],[38],[39]) to analyze systems in similar settings. We will consider (2.2) along with the boundary conditions

∂n∂ν=∂z∂ν=0,andu=0for ​x∈∂Ω⁡ and ​t>0,\displaystyle\frac{\partial n}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial\nu}=0,\quad\text{and}\quad u=0\quad\text{for }x\in\romega\text{ and }t>0, (2.18)

and initial conditions

n⁡(x,0)=n0​(x),z⁡(x,0)=z0​(x):=−ln⁡(c0​(x)‖c0‖L∞​(Ω)),u=u0​(x),x∈Ω.\displaystyle n(x,0)=n_{0}(x),\quad z(x,0)=z_{0}(x):=-\ln\left(\frac{c_{0}(x)}{\|c_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}}\right),\quad u=u_{0}(x),\quad x\in\Omega.
Remark 2.4.

Let f∈C3​([0,∞))f\in C^{3}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) satisfy (2.5). Assume that (n,z,u)∈C2,1​(Ω¯×(T1,T2))(n,z,u)\in C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times(T_{1},T_{2})\right) is a classical solution of the boundary value problem (2.2),(2.18) in Ω×(T1,T2)\Omega\times(T_{1},T_{2}) with some T1≥0T_{1}\geq 0 and T2∈(T1,∞]T_{2}\in(T_{1},\infty]. Then the solution satisfies the mass conservation property

dd⁡t​∫Ωn⁡(⋅,t)=0for all ​t∈(T1,T2).\displaystyle\frac{\intd}{\intd t}\int_{\Omega}\!n(\cdot,t)=0\quad\text{for all }t\in(T_{1},T_{2}).

This reformulation of our previous generalized systems at hand, we immediately obtain the following basic information – not depending on ff – about the transformed chemical concentration zz.

Lemma 2.5.

Let m0>0m_{0}>0. Suppose that for f∈C3​([0,∞))f\in C^{3}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) satisfying (2.5) and t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0 the triple (n,z,u)∈C2,1​(Ω¯×(t0,∞))(n,z,u)\in C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times(t_{0},\infty)\right) is a classical solution of (2.2)–(2.18) in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) with the properties that n≥0n\geq 0 in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) and ∫Ωn⁡(⋅,t0)≤m0\int_{\Omega}\!n(\cdot,t_{0})\leq m_{0}. Then

∫Ωz⁡(⋅,t)+∫t0t∫Ω|∇z|2≤∫Ωz⁡(⋅,t0)+(t−t0)​m0for all ​t>t0.\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!z(\cdot,t)+\int_{t_{0}}^{t}\!\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{2}\leq\int_{\Omega}\!z(\cdot,t_{0})+(t-t_{0})m_{0}\quad\text{for all }t>t_{0}. (2.19)

Integrating the second equation of (2.2) with respect to space shows that

dd⁡t​∫Ωz=∫ΩΔ​z−∫Ω|∇z|2+∫Ωf⁡(n)+∫Ωu⋅∇z\displaystyle\frac{\intd}{\intd t}\int_{\Omega}\!z=\int_{\Omega}\!\Delta z-\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{2}+\int_{\Omega}\!f(n)+\int_{\Omega}\!u\cdot\nabla z

holds for all t∈(t0,∞)t\in(t_{0},\infty). Making use of ∇⁣⋅⁡u=0\dive u=0, the Neumann boundary conditions for zz, n≥0n\geq 0 and the fact that f⁡(s)≤sf(s)\leq s for all s≥0s\geq 0 we obtain, upon integration by parts, that

dd⁡t​∫Ωz+∫Ω|∇z|2≤∫Ωn\displaystyle\frac{\intd}{\intd t}\int_{\Omega}\!z+\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{2}\leq\int_{\Omega}\!n

is valid on t∈(0,∞)t\in(0,\infty). Due to the mass conservation we have ∫Ωn⁡(⋅,t)≤m0\int_{\Omega}\!n(\cdot,t)\leq m_{0} for all t>t0t>t_{0} and therefore integrating this inequality immediately establishes (2.19). ∎

3 Generalized solution concept and approximate solutions

Before going into more detail for our eventual smoothness result, let us briefly review the solution concept of generalized solutions and the exact form of the approximate problems. These were already used in [36, 38] for the closely related settings without fluid and in [30] for the system with Stokes fluid.

A global generalized solution is defined as follows (see also [36, Definition 2.1–2.3],[30, Definition 2.1]).

Definition 3.1.

Assume that (n0,c0,u0)(n_{0},c_{0},u_{0}) satisfy (1). Suppose that a triple (n,c,u)(n,c,u) of functions

{n∈Ll​o​c1​(Ω¯×[0,∞)),c∈Ll​o​c∞​(Ω¯×[0,∞))∩Ll​o​c2​([0,∞),W1,2​(Ω)),u∈Ll​o​c1​([0,∞),W01,1​(Ω),ℝ2),\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{l@{\, }c@{\, }l}n&\in&L_{loc}^{1}\!\left(\bomega\times[0,\infty)\right),\\ c&\in&L_{loc}^{\infty}\!\left(\bomega\times[0,\infty)\right)\cap L_{loc}^{2}\!\left([0,\infty);W^{1,2}(\Omega)\right),\\ u&\in&L^{1}_{loc}\big([0,\infty);W^{1,1}_{0}\left(\Omega\right);\mathbb{R}^{2}\big),\end{array}\right.

satisfies

n≥0,andc>0,and∇⁣⋅⁡u=0a.e. in ​Ω×(0,∞),\displaystyle n\geq 0,\quad\text{and}\quad c>0,\quad\text{and}\quad\dive u=0\quad\text{a.e. in }\Omega\times(0,\infty), (3.4)

as well as

∇ln⁡(n+1)∈Ll​o​c2​(Ω¯×[0,∞))and∇ln⁡c∈Ll​o​c2​(Ω¯×[0,∞)).\displaystyle\nabla\ln(n+1)\in L_{loc}^{2}\!\left(\bomega\times[0,\infty)\right)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\nabla\ln c\in L_{loc}^{2}\!\left(\bomega\times[0,\infty)\right). (3.5)

Then (n,c,u)(n,c,u) will be called a global generalized solution of (1)– (1.12) if nn satisfies the mass conservation property

∫Ωn⁡(x,t)​d⁡x=∫Ωn0​(x)​d⁡xfor a.e. ​t>0,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!n(x,t)\intd x=\int_{\Omega}\!n_{0}(x)\intd x\quad\text{for a.e. }t>0,

if the inequality

−\displaystyle- ∫0∞∫Ωln⁡(n+1)​φt−∫Ωln⁡(n0+1)​φ​(⋅,0)\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!\ln(n+1)\varphi_{t}-\int_{\Omega}\!\ln(n_{0}+1)\varphi(\cdot,0)
≥∫0∞∫Ω|∇ln(n+1)|2φ−∫0∞∫Ω∇ln(n+1)⋅∇φ+∫0∞∫Ωnn+1∇lnc⋅∇φ\displaystyle\geq\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla\ln(n+1)|^{2}\varphi-\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!\nabla\ln(n+1)\cdot\nabla\varphi+\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!\frac{n}{n+1}\nabla\ln c\cdot\nabla\varphi (3.6)
−∫0∞∫Ωnn+1(∇ln(n+1)⋅∇lnc)φ+∫0∞∫Ωln(n+1)(u⋅∇φ)\displaystyle\quad-\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!\frac{n}{n+1}\left(\nabla\ln(n+1)\cdot\nabla\ln c\right)\varphi+\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!\ln(n+1)(u\cdot\nabla\varphi)

holds for each nonnegative φ∈C0∞​(Ω¯×[0,∞))\varphi\in C^{\infty}_{0}\left(\bomega\times[0,\infty)\right), if the identity

∫0∞∫Ωc​ψt+∫Ωc0​ψ​(⋅,0)=∫0∞∫Ω∇c⋅∇ψ+∫0∞∫Ωn​c​ψ−∫0∞∫Ωc​u⋅∇ψ\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!c\psi_{t}+\int_{\Omega}\!c_{0}\psi(\cdot,0)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!\nabla c\cdot\nabla\psi+\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!nc\psi-\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!cu\cdot\nabla\psi

is valid for any ψ∈L∞​(Ω×(0,∞))∩L​((0,∞),W1,2​(Ω))\psi\in L^{\infty\;\!}\!\left(\Omega\times(0,\infty)\right)\cap L^{2\;\!}\!\left((0,\infty);W^{1,2}(\Omega)\right) compactly supported in Ω¯×[0,∞)\bomega\times[0,\infty) with ψt∈L​(Ω×(0,∞))\psi_{t}\in L^{2\;\!}\!\left(\Omega\times(0,\infty)\right), and if furthermore the equality

∫0∞∫Ωu⋅Ψt+∫Ωu0⋅Ψ(⋅,0)=∫0∞∫Ω∇u⋅∇Ψ−∫0∞∫Ωn∇ϕ⋅Ψ\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!u\cdot\Psi_{t}+\int_{\Omega}\!u_{0}\cdot\Psi(\cdot,0)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!\nabla u\cdot\nabla\Psi-\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\Omega}\!n\nabla\phi\cdot\Psi

holds for all Ψ∈C0,σ∞​(Ω×[0,∞))\Psi\in C_{0,\sigma}^{\infty}\left(\Omega\times[0,\infty)\right).

It can easily be verified that the supersolution property in (3.6) combined with the mass conservation (2.9) is sufficient to obtain that sufficiently regular global generalized solutions are also global solutions in the classical sense (see [38, Remark 2.1 ii)]), i.e. if (n,c,u)(n,c,u) is a global generalized solution in the sense of Definition 3.1 and satisfies n≥0n\geq 0 and c>0c>0 in Ω¯×[0,∞)\bomega\times[0,\infty) as well as (n,c,u)∈C0​(Ω¯×[0,∞))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,∞))(n,c,u)\in\!C^{0}\!\left(\bomega\times[0,\infty)\right)\cap C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times(0,\infty)\right) then (n,c,u)(n,c,u) solves (2) in the classical sense.

Generalized solutions in the sense of Definition 3.1 are constructed by an approximation procedure relying on regularizations in the form of (2.2) with suitably chosen f≡fεf\equiv f_{\varepsilon} ([38, 39, 30]). For this we first fix a cut-off function ρ∈C∞​([0,∞))\rho\in C^{\infty}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) fulfilling ρ≡1\rho\equiv 1 in [0,1][0,1] and ρ≡0\rho\equiv 0 in [2,∞)[2,\infty) and define the family of functions {fε}ε∈(0,1)⊆C∞​([0,∞))\left\{f_{\varepsilon}\right\}_{\varepsilon\in(0,1)}\subseteq C^{\infty}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) given by

fε​(s):=∫0sρ⁡(ε​σ)​d⁡σ,s≥0.\displaystyle f_{\varepsilon}(s):=\int_{0}^{s}\rho(\varepsilon\sigma)\intd\sigma,\qquad s\geq 0. (3.7)

Every function in this family evidently has the properties

fε(0)=0 and 0≤fε′≤1 on [0,∞),\displaystyle f_{\varepsilon}(0)=0\quad\text{ and }\quad 0\leq f^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\leq 1\quad\text{ on }[0,\infty), (3.8)

as well as

fε​(s)=sfor all ​s∈[0,1ε] and fε′​(s)=0for all ​s≥2ε.\displaystyle f_{\varepsilon}(s)=s\quad\text{for all }s\in[0,\textstyle\frac{1}{\varepsilon}]\quad\text{ and }\quad f^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}(s)=0\quad\text{for all }s\geq\frac{2}{\varepsilon}.

Furthermore it holds that

fε​(s)↗sandfε′​(s)↗1as ​ε↘0\displaystyle f_{\varepsilon}(s)\nearrow s\quad\text{and}\quad f^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}(s)\nearrow 1\quad\text{as }\varepsilon\searrow 0

for each s≥0s\geq 0. According to this choice we can ensure that for the local solutions to (2) –(2.7) nεn_{\varepsilon} is bounded throughout Ω×(0,Tm​a​x)\Omega\times(0,T_{max}), and that cεc_{\varepsilon} is strictly positive on Ω¯×(0,Tmax)\bomega\times(0,T_{max}), meaning that the most troublesome terms of the extensibility criterion in (2.8) remain bounded, whence the further estimation of remaining less troublesome terms in fact shows that the solution actually is global ([30]).

Relying on the logarithmic transformation again we obtain for this family of regularizing functions, (2.2)– (2.18) systems of the form

{nε​t+uε⋅∇nε=Δnε+∇⋅(nεf′ε(nε)∇zε),x∈Ω,t>0,zε​t−uε⋅∇zε=Δ​zε−|∇zε|2+fε​(nε),x∈Ω,t>0,uε​t+∇Pε=Δuε+nε∇ϕ,x∈Ω,t>0,∇⁣⋅⁡uε=0,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{r@{\,}c@{\,}c@{\,}l@{\quad}l@{\quad}l@{\,}c}n_{\varepsilon t}&+&u_{\varepsilon}\cdot\!\nabla n_{\varepsilon}&=\Delta n_{\varepsilon}+\nabla\!\cdot(n_{\varepsilon}f^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}(n_{\varepsilon})\nabla z_{\varepsilon}),&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ z_{\varepsilon t}&-&u_{\varepsilon}\cdot\!\nabla z_{\varepsilon}&=\Delta z_{\varepsilon}-|\nabla z_{\varepsilon}|^{2}+f_{\varepsilon}(n_{\varepsilon}),&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ u_{\varepsilon t}&+&\nabla P_{\varepsilon}&=\Delta u_{\varepsilon}+n_{\varepsilon}\nabla\phi,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\\ &&\dive u_{\varepsilon}&=0,&x\in\Omega,&t>0,\end{array}\right.

with boundary conditions

∂nε∂ν=∂zε∂ν=0,anduε=0for ​x∈∂Ω⁡ and ​t>0,\displaystyle\frac{\partial n_{\varepsilon}}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial z_{\varepsilon}}{\partial\nu}=0,\quad\text{and}\quad u_{\varepsilon}=0\quad\text{for }x\in\romega\text{ and }t>0, (3.13)

and initial conditions

According to [30] also these problems posses global classical solutions, with again nεn_{\varepsilon} and zεz_{\varepsilon} being nonnegative, nεn_{\varepsilon} still satisfying the mass conservation property as in Remark 2.4 and (nε,zε,uε)(n_{\varepsilon},z_{\varepsilon},u_{\varepsilon}) correspond to solutions of systems of the form (2) by means of the substitution zε=−ln⁡(cε‖c0‖L∞​(Ω))z_{\varepsilon}=-\ln\left(\frac{c_{\varepsilon}}{\|c_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}}\right).

The following result summarizes the result on approximation of the generalized solutions established in [30, Lemma 2.5].

Lemma 3.2.

Let (1) hold and denote by (n,c,u)(n,c,u) the global generalized solution of (1)– (1.12) from Theorem A. Then there exists a sequence {εj}j∈ℕ⊂(0,1)\{\varepsilon_{j}\}_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\subset(0,1) such that εj↘0\varepsilon_{j}\searrow 0 as j→∞j\to\infty and such that, for the choice of f≡fεf\equiv f_{\varepsilon} in (2), the corresponding solution (nε,cε,uε)(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon},u_{\varepsilon}) of (2)– (2.7) satisfies

nε→n,andcε→c,as well asuε→ua.e. in ​Ω×(0,∞).\displaystyle n_{\varepsilon}\to n,\qquad\text{and}\qquad c_{\varepsilon}\to c,\qquad\text{as well as}\qquad u_{\varepsilon}\to u\qquad\text{a.e. in }\Omega\times(0,\infty).

as ε=εj↘0\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{j}\searrow 0.

4 Eventual smoothness of small-data generalized solutions

4.1 Nonincreasing energy for small mass

We will appropriately adjust the functional methods employed in [39] to our needs. In fact we will study the behavior of functionals of the form

Fμ​(n,z):=∫Ωn​ln⁡nμ+12​∫Ω|∇z|2\displaystyle F_{\mu}(n,z):=\int_{\Omega}\!n\ln\frac{n}{\mu}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{2} (4.1)

for μ>0\mu>0, 0≤n∈C0​(Ω¯)0\leq n\in C^{0}\!\left(\bomega\right) and z∈C1​(Ω¯)z\in C^{1}\!\left(\bomega\right). We will show that a suitable condition on the size of Fμ​(n⁡(⋅,t0),z⁡(⋅,t0))F_{\mu}\big(n(\cdot,t_{0}),z(\cdot,t_{0})\big) for some t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0 implies that FμF_{\mu} is non-increasing from that time onward, along the trajectory of classical solutions to the system (2.2). Since we are working with the more generalized version of (3) almost all of the properties of FμF_{\mu} also hold in our limit case f⁡(ξ)≡ξf(\xi)\equiv\xi obtained by taking ε↘0\varepsilon\searrow 0 in (3). In particular, this will also hold true for the conditional regularity estimates discussed in Section 4.2.

We start with some basic relations between FμF_{\mu} and the quantities appearing therein.

Lemma 4.1.

For μ>0\mu>0 let FμF_{\mu} be given by (4.1). Then for all nonnegative n∈C0​(Ω¯)n\in C^{0}\!\left(\bomega\right) and any z∈C1​(Ω¯)z\in C^{1}\!\left(\bomega\right) we have

∫Ωn​|ln⁡n|≤Fμ​(n,z)+ln⁡μ​∫Ωn+2​|Ω|e,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!n|\ln n|\leq F_{\mu}(n,z)+\ln\mu\int_{\Omega}\!n+\frac{2|\Omega|}{e}, (4.2)

and

∫Ω|∇z|2\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{2} ≤2​Fμ​(n,z)+2​μ​|Ω|e,\displaystyle\leq 2F_{\mu}(n,z)+\frac{2\mu|\Omega|}{e}, (4.3)

as well as

Fμ​(n,z)≥−μ​|Ω|e.\displaystyle F_{\mu}(n,z)\geq-\frac{\mu|\Omega|}{e}. (4.4)
Proof:

Making use of the facts that nn is nonnegative and that −ξ​ln⁡ξ≤1e-\xi\ln\xi\leq\frac{1}{e} for all ξ>0\xi>0 we can see that

∫Ωn​|ln⁡n|\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!n|\ln n| =Fμ(n,z)−12∫Ω|∇z|2+lnμ∫Ωn−2∫{n<1}nlnn≤Fμ(n,z)+lnμ∫Ωn+2​|Ω|e,\displaystyle=F_{\mu}(n,z)-\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{2}+\ln\mu\int_{\Omega}\!n-2\int_{\{n<1\}}n\ln n\leq F_{\mu}(n,z)+\ln\mu\int_{\Omega}\!n+\frac{2|\Omega|}{e},

proving (4.2). Similarly, we may compute

12​∫Ω|∇z|2=Fμ​(n,z)−μ​∫Ωnμ​ln⁡nμ≤Fμ​(n,z)+μ​|Ω|e,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{2}=F_{\mu}(n,z)-\mu\int_{\Omega}\!\frac{n}{\mu}\ln\frac{n}{\mu}\leq F_{\mu}(n,z)+\frac{\mu|\Omega|}{e},

which first proves (4.3) and, upon reordering and dropping the nonnegative term, also (4.4). ∎

The main ingredient in showing that this generalized energy is non-increasing (after some waiting time) will be the following differential inequality.

Lemma 4.2.

Let m>0m>0 and T≥0T\geq 0 and assume that for f∈C3​([0,∞))f\in C^{3}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) satisfying (2.5) the triple (n,z,u)∈C2,1​(Ω¯×(T,∞))(n,z,u)\in C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times(T,\infty)\right) is a classical solution of (2.2)– (2.18) in Ω×(T,∞)\Omega\times(T,\infty) satisfying ∫Ω|u⁡(⋅,T)|4≤ℓ\int_{\Omega}\!|u(\cdot,T)|^{4}\leq\ell, and ∫Ωn⁡(⋅,t)≤m\int_{\Omega}\!n(\cdot,t)\leq m for all t>Tt>T, as well as n>0n>0 in Ω×(T,∞)\Omega\times(T,\infty). +{12−K32∫Ω|∇z(⋅,t)|2−K32Ku|Ω|14(ℓe−λ1​(t−T)+m)}∫Ω|Δz(⋅,t)|2≤0\displaystyle+\left\{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{K_{3}}{2}\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z(\cdot,t)|^{2}-K_{3}^{2}K_{u}|\Omega|^{\frac{1}{4}}\big(\ell e^{-\lambda_{1}(t-T)}+m\big)\right\}\int_{\Omega}\!|\Delta z(\cdot,t)|^{2}\leq 0

for all t>Tt>T, with K3K_{3} as in (1.23) and KuK_{u}, λ1\lambda_{1} provided by Lemma 2.2.

≤K32​Ku​|Ω|14​(ℓ​e−λ1​(t−T)+m)​∫Ω|Δ​z|2for all ​t>T,\displaystyle\leq K_{3}^{2}K_{u}|\Omega|^{\frac{1}{4}}\big(\ell e^{-\lambda_{1}(t-T)}+m\big)\int_{\Omega}\!|\Delta z|^{2}\quad\text{for all }t>T, (4.7)

since ∫Ωn≤m\int_{\Omega}\!n\leq m in (T,∞)(T,\infty). Combining (4.5)–(4.7) and reordering appropriately completes the proof. ∎

In view of the lemma above, the possibility for an inequality of the form dd⁡tFμ(n(⋅,t),z(⋅,))≤0\frac{\intd}{\intd t}F_{\mu}\big(n(\cdot,t),z(\cdot,)\big)\leq 0 will depend on the nonnegativity of the term 12−K32​∫Ω|∇z​(⋅,t)|2−K32​Ku​|Ω|14​(ℓ​e−λ1​t+m)\frac{1}{2}-\frac{K_{3}}{2}\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z(\cdot,t)|^{2}-K_{3}^{2}K_{u}|\Omega|^{\frac{1}{4}}(\ell e^{-\lambda_{1}t}+m). 4.2 Conditional regularity estimates

In this section we will establish appropriate Hölder bounds for the components of our approximate solutions under the assumption that we already have control of ∫Ω|∇z|p\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{p} for some p>2p>2. In fact, as we will see in Section 4.3, obtaining the bound assumed throughout the section for the special value of p=4p=4, will only require bounds on ∫Ωn​|ln⁡n|\int_{\Omega}\!n|\ln n| and ∫Ω|∇z|2\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{2}, which (at least for possibly large times) can be obtained by relying on our analysis of FμF_{\mu} (see Section 4.4). Our arguments here are inspired an approach illustrated in [39, Section 4.2 and 4.3].

Lemma 4.4.

Let p>2p>2, m0>0m_{0}>0, M>0M>0 and τ>0\tau>0. Then there exists C=C⁡(p,m0,M,τ)>0C=C(p,m_{0},M,\tau)>0 such that if for f∈C3​([0,∞))f\in C^{3}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) satisfying (2.5) and some t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0 the triple (n,z,u)∈C2,1​(Ω¯×(t0,∞))(n,z,u)\in C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times(t_{0},\infty)\right) is a classical solution of (2.2)–(2.18) in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) satisfying n≥0n\geq 0 in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) and

∫Ωn⁡(⋅,t0)≤m0\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!n(\cdot,t_{0})\leq m_{0} (4.15)

as well as

∫Ω|∇z​(⋅,t)|p≤Mfor all ​t>t0,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z(\cdot,t)|^{p}\leq M\quad\text{for all }t>t_{0},

then

‖n⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤Cfor all ​t≥t0+τ.\displaystyle\|n(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq C\quad\text{for all }t\geq t_{0}+\tau. (4.16)
Proof:

The proof is based on arguments employed in e.g. [39, Lemma 4.4]. We let T>t0+1T>t_{0}+1 and define

S⁡(T):=max⁡{S1,S2​(T)}\displaystyle S(T):=\max\left\{S_{1},S_{2}(T)\right\}

with

S1:=maxt∈[t0,t0+1]⁡(t−t0)​‖n⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)andS2​(T):=maxt∈[t0+1,T]⁡‖n⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω).\displaystyle S_{1}:=\max_{t\in[t_{0},t_{0}+1]}(t-t_{0})\|n(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\quad\text{and}\quad S_{2}(T):=\max_{t\in[t_{0}+1,T]}\|n(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}.

Now, in order to estimate S⁡(T)S(T) from above, we let t1​(t):=max⁡{t−1,t0}t_{1}(t):=\max\{t-1,t_{0}\} and for t∈(t0,T)t\in(t_{0},T) represent n⁡(⋅,t)n(\cdot,t) according to

n⁡(⋅,t)\displaystyle n(\cdot,t) =e(t−t1)​Δn(⋅,t1)+∫t1te(t−s)​Δ[∇⋅(n(⋅,s)f′(n(⋅,s))∇z(⋅,s))−(u(⋅,s)⋅∇n(⋅,s))]ds\displaystyle=e^{(t-t_{1})\Delta}n(\cdot,t_{1})+\!\int_{t_{1}}^{t}\!\!e^{(t-s)\Delta}\Big[\nabla\cdot\!\big(n(\cdot,s)f^{\prime}(n(\cdot,s))\nabla z(\cdot,s)\big)-\big(u(\cdot,s)\cdot\!\nabla n(\cdot,s)\big)\Big]\intd s
=:e(t−t1)​Δ​n​(⋅,t1)+I⁡(t1,t),\displaystyle=:e^{(t-t_{1})\Delta}n(\cdot,t_{1})+I(t_{1},t), (4.17)

Lemma 4.6.

Let p>2p>2, m0>0m_{0}>0, m1>0m_{1}>0, M>0M>0 and T>0T>0. Then there exists C=C⁡(p,m0,m1,M,T)>0C=C(p,m_{0},m_{1},M,T)>0 such that if for f∈C3​([0,∞))f\in C^{3}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) satisfying (2.5) and t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0 the triple (n,z,u)∈C0​(Ω¯×[t0,∞))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(t0,∞))(n,z,u)\in C^{0}\!\left(\bomega\times[t_{0},\infty)\right)\cap C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times(t_{0},\infty)\right) is a classical solution of (2.2)–(2.18) in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) with the properties that n≥0n\geq 0 in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) and

∫Ωn⁡(⋅,t)≤m0for all ​t>t0,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!n(\cdot,t)\leq m_{0}\quad\text{for all }t>t_{0}, (4.28)

and

as well as

z⁡(x,t)≤Cfor all ​x∈Ω​and​t∈(t0,T).\displaystyle z(x,t)\leq C\quad\text{for all }x\in\Omega\ \text{and}\ t\in(t_{0},T).

|φ⁡(x)−φ⁡(y)|≤C1​|x−y|1−2p​‖∇φ‖Lp​(Ω)for all ​x,y∈Ω.\displaystyle|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)|\leq C_{1}|x-y|^{1-\frac{2}{p}}\|\nabla\varphi\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)}\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\Omega. (4.31)

z⁡(x0​(t),t)≤m1+m0​T|Ω|.\displaystyle z(x_{0}(t),t)\leq\frac{m_{1}+m_{0}T}{|\Omega|}.

z⁡(x,t)\displaystyle z(x,t) ≤z⁡(x0​(t),t)+|z⁡(x,t)−z⁡(x0​(t),t)|\displaystyle\leq z(x_{0}(t),t)+\big|z(x,t)-z(x_{0}(t),t)\big|
≤m1+m0​T|Ω|+C1​|x−x0​(t)|1−2p​‖∇z​(⋅,t)‖Lp​(Ω)\displaystyle\leq\frac{m_{1}+m_{0}T}{|\Omega|}+C_{1}|x-x_{0}(t)|^{1-\frac{2}{p}}\|\nabla z(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)}

Drawing on the now proven time-local bound for zz, we can rely on the Hölder estimates for nn and uu and well known parabolic regularity theory to the following set of further bounds.

Lemma 4.7.

Let p>2,m0>0,m1>0,M>0,T>0p>2,m_{0}>0,m_{1}>0,M>0,T>0 and τ>0\tau>0. Then there exist θ=θ⁡(p)∈(0,1)\theta=\theta(p)\in(0,1) and C=C⁡(p,m0,m1,M,T,τ)>0C=C(p,m_{0},m_{1},M,T,\tau)>0 such that if for f∈C3​([0,∞))f\in C^{3}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) satisfying (2.5) and t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0 the triple (n,z,u)∈C0​(Ω¯×[t0,∞))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(t0,∞))(n,z,u)\in C^{0}\!\left(\bomega\times[t_{0},\infty)\right)\cap C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times(t_{0},\infty)\right) is a classical solution of (2.2)–(2.18) in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) with the properties that n≥0n\geq 0 and z≥0z\geq 0 in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) and

∫Ωn⁡(⋅,t0)≤m0,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!n(\cdot,t_{0})\leq m_{0},

and

∫Ωz⁡(⋅,t0)≤m1,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!z(\cdot,t_{0})\leq m_{1},

as well as

∫Ω|∇z​(⋅,t)|p≤Mfor all ​t>t0,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z(\cdot,t)|^{p}\leq M\quad\text{for all }t>t_{0},

then

‖n‖C2+θ,1+θ2​(Ω¯×[t0+τ,T])≤C,‖z‖C2+θ,1+θ2​(Ω¯×[t0+τ,T])≤C,‖u‖C2+θ,1+θ2​(Ω¯×[t0+τ,T])≤C.\displaystyle\|n\|_{C^{2+\theta,1+\frac{\theta}{2}}\!\left(\bomega\times[t_{0}+\tau,T]\right)}\leq C,\quad\|z\|_{C^{2+\theta,1+\frac{\theta}{2}}\!\left(\bomega\times[t_{0}+\tau,T]\right)}\leq C,\quad\|u\|_{C^{2+\theta,1+\frac{\theta}{2}}\!\left(\bomega\times[t_{0}+\tau,T]\right)}\leq C. (4.32)
Proof:

By Lemma 4.6 and the fact that zz is nonnegative we have

0≤z≤C1in ​Ω×(t0,T)\displaystyle 0\leq z\leq C_{1}\quad\text{in }\Omega\times(t_{0},T)

with some C1=C1​(p,m0,m1,M,T)>0C_{1}=C_{1}(p,m_{0},m_{1},M,T)>0. Thus, letting c~:=e−z\tilde{c}:=e^{-z} we obtain

e−C1≤c~≤1in ​Ω×(t0,T).\displaystyle e^{-C_{1}}\leq\tilde{c}\leq 1\quad\text{in }\Omega\times(t_{0},T). (4.33)

Furthermore, c~\tilde{c} solves the Neumann boundary value problem c~t=Δc~+u∇c~−f(n)c~\tilde{c}_{t}=\Delta\tilde{c}+u\nabla\tilde{c}-f(n)\tilde{c} in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) with Hölder continuous coefficients, since Lemma 4.5 entails the existence of θ1∈(0,1)\theta_{1}\in(0,1) and C2=C2​(p,m0,M,τ)>0C_{2}=C_{2}(p,m_{0},M,\tau)>0 such that

‖n‖Cθ1,θ12​(Ω¯×[t0+τ4,T])+‖u‖Cθ1,θ12​(Ω¯×[t0+τ4,T])≤C2.\displaystyle\|n\|_{C^{\theta_{1},\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}}\!\left(\bomega\times[t_{0}+\frac{\tau}{4},T]\right)}+\|u\|_{C^{\theta_{1},\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}}\!\left(\bomega\times[t_{0}+\frac{\tau}{4},T]\right)}\leq C_{2}.

Hence, according to standard parabolic Schauder theory ([14, III.5.1 and IV.5.3]), there exists some θ2∈(0,1)\theta_{2}\in(0,1) and C3=C3​(p,m0,m1,M,T,τ)C_{3}=C_{3}(p,m_{0},m_{1},M,T,\tau) such that

‖c~‖C2+θ2,1+θ22​(Ω¯×[t0+τ2,T])≤C3,\displaystyle\|\tilde{c}\|_{C^{2+\theta_{2},1+\frac{\theta_{2}}{2}}\!\left(\bomega\times[t_{0}+\frac{\tau}{2},T]\right)}\leq C_{3},

yielding the regularity assertion for zz featured in (4.32) due to the lower bound for c~\tilde{c} in (4.33). Relying on parabolic Schauder theory once more, we can conclude from the first equation that also nn satisfies (4.32). That also uu satisfies (4.32) can be readily obtained by well known smoothing properties of the Stokes operator (see eg. [8, Theorem 2.8], [2, Theorem 1.1]) and the boundedness of nn established in Lemma 4.4. ∎

4.3 Conditional estimates for ∫Ω|∇z|4\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{4} and ∫Ωn2\int_{\Omega}\!n^{2}

In this section we will focus on obtaining a bound on ∫Ω|∇z|4\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{4}, which in view of Section 4.2 is the main requirement for the regularity estimates we will depend on later. As a preliminary step we derive some basic differential inequalities through standard testing procedures.

Lemma 4.8.

Suppose that for f∈C3​([0,∞))f\in C^{3}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) satisfying (2.5) and t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0 the triple (n,z,u)∈C2,1​(Ω¯×(t0,∞))(n,z,u)\in C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times(t_{0},\infty)\right) is a classical solution of (2.2)– (2.18) in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty). Then

By simply testing the first equation of (2.2) with nn, we can rely on integration by parts, one application of Young’s inequality, and the fact |f′​(n)|≤1|f^{\prime}(n)|\leq 1 to easily arrive at (4.34). ∎

holds for all t>t0t>t_{0}.

We differentiate the second equation of (2.2) with regard to space and multiply by |∇z|2∇z|\nabla z|^{2}\nabla z. Combination of the two prepared inequalities will now result in the desired bounds for ∫Ω|∇z|4\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{4} and ∫Ωn2\int_{\Omega}\!n^{2}, if we assume that we already have suitable bounds for the quantities ∫Ωn​ln⁡n\int_{\Omega}\!n\ln n and ∫Ω|∇z|2\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{2}. Lemma 4.10.

Let K2K_{2} be as in (1.22). Then for all m0>0m_{0}>0, each L>0L>0 and any M∈(0,14​K2)M\in\big(0,\frac{1}{4K_{2}}\big) and τ>0\tau>0 there exists C>0C>0 such that if for f∈C3​([0,∞))f\in C^{3}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) satisfying (2.5) and some t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0 the triple (n,z,u)∈C2,1​(Ω¯×(t0,∞))(n,z,u)\in C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times(t_{0},\infty)\right) is a classical solution of (2.2)– (2.18) in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) satisfying n≥0n\geq 0 in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) and

as well as

∫Ωn⁡(⋅,t)​|ln⁡n⁡(⋅,t)|≤Land∫Ω|∇z​(⋅,t)|2≤Mfor all ​t>t0,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!n(\cdot,t)|\ln n(\cdot,t)|\leq L\quad\text{and}\quad\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z(\cdot,t)|^{2}\leq M\quad\text{for all }t>t_{0}, (4.42)

∫Ωn2​(⋅,t)≤Cand∫Ω|∇z​(⋅,t)|4≤Cfor all ​t≥t0+τ.\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!n^{2}(\cdot,t)\leq C\quad\text{and}\quad\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z(\cdot,t)|^{4}\leq C\quad\text{for all }t\geq t_{0}+\tau. (4.43)

Now, assuming (4.41) and (4.42) to hold, we combine the inequalites established in Lemma 4.8 and Lemma 4.9 to obtain

≤\displaystyle\leq\quad (1+12η)​∫Ωn2​|∇z|2+8​∫Ω|∇z|6+4​∫Ω|∇z|4​|∇u|+C1​M2for all ​t>t0,\displaystyle\Big(1+\frac{12}{\eta}\Big)\int_{\Omega}\!n^{2}|\nabla z|^{2}+8\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{6}+4\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{4}|\nabla u|+C_{1}M^{2}\quad\text{for all }t>t_{0},

To further control the term containing n3n^{3}, we recall that by a variant of the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality (c.f. [3, (22)]) and Remark 2.4 we have

with some C3>0C_{3}>0. Returning to the analyzation of the remaining terms in (4.45), we observe that by Hölder’s inequality, Lemma 2.3 combined with (4.41), the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality, and finally Young’s inequality we can find C4,C5,C6>0C_{4},C_{5},C_{6}>0 such that

≤C5​(∫Ω|∇|∇z|2|2)5/6​(∫Ω|∇z|2)1/3+C5​(∫Ω|∇z|2)2\displaystyle\leq C_{5}\left(\int_{\Omega}\!\big|\nabla|\nabla z|^{2}\big|^{2}\right)^{\nicefrac{{5}}{{6}}}\left(\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{2}\right)^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{3}}}+C_{5}\left(\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z|^{2}\right)^{2}
≤12​∫Ω|∇|∇z|2|2+C6​M2for all ​t>t0.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}\!\big|\nabla|\nabla z|^{2}\big|^{2}+C_{6}M^{2}\quad\text{for all }t>t_{0}. (4.48)

and therefore

Collecting (4.46)–(4.49), we infer from (4.45) that for some C8>0C_{8}>0 we have

for some C9>0C_{9}>0, and secondly, relying on (4.42), we find C10>0C_{10}>0 such that

For the our next proof we will require the following result demonstrated in [30, Lemma 2.6], which is based on an application the Trudinger-Moser inequality combined with a spatio-temporal estimate on ∇ln⁡(nε+1)\nabla\ln(n_{\varepsilon}+1) in L2L^{2}.

4.5 Stabilization of solutions with small energy

This section discusses the last missing part for the proof of Theorem 1.1, which is the convergence properties featured therein. Since from the last section we already known, that our generalized solutions will be classical solutions after some waiting time, we will concern our investigation only with convergence of classical solutions to (2.2). Before proving the desired large time behavior we require one additional preparation in form of a time-independent Hölder bound from ∇z\nabla z.

Lemma 4.14.

For all m0>0m_{0}>0, M>0M>0, τ>0\tau>0 there exist θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) and C>0C>0 such that if for f∈C3​([0,∞))f\in C^{3}\!\left([0,\infty)\right) satisfying (2.5) and t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0 the triple (n,z,u)∈C0​(Ω¯×[t0,∞))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(t0,∞))(n,z,u)\in C^{0}\!\left(\bomega\times[t_{0},\infty)\right)\cap C^{2,1}\!\left(\bomega\times(t_{0},\infty)\right) is a classical solution of (2.2)– (2.18) in Ω×(t0,∞)\Omega\times(t_{0},\infty) satisfying

∫Ωn⁡(⋅,t0)≤m0,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!n(\cdot,t_{0})\leq m_{0},

and

∫Ω|∇z​(⋅,t)|4≤Mfor all ​t>t0,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\!|\nabla z(\cdot,t)|^{4}\leq M\quad\text{for all }t>t_{0},

it holds that

‖∇z​(⋅,t)‖Cθ​(Ω¯)≤Cfor all ​t≥t0+τ.\displaystyle\|\nabla z(\cdot,t)\|_{C^{\theta}\!\,\left(\bomega\right)}\leq C\quad\text{for all }t\geq t_{0}+\tau. (4.69)
Proof:

Proof of Theorem 1.1:.

With m⋆>0m_{\star}>0 provided by Lemma 4.12 we obtain from Proposition 4.13 that for any initial data (n0,c0,u0)(n_{0},c_{0},u_{0}) satisfying (1) as well as (1.17), there exists T>0T>0 such that the solution (n,c,u)(n,c,u) from Theorem A has the regularity properties featured in (1.18) and the positivity of cc in Ω¯×(T,∞)\bomega\times(T,\infty) as claimed in (1.19) are valid. Since (4.67) from Proposition 4.13 furthermore guarantees that inft>TFμ​(n⁡(⋅,t),z⁡(⋅,t))<14​K3−μ​|Ω|e\inf_{t>T}F_{\mu}\big(n(\cdot,t),z(\cdot,t)\big)<\tfrac{1}{4K_{3}}-\tfrac{\mu|\Omega|}{e}, we may employ Proposition 4.15 to obtain (1.20) and (1.21). ∎

4.6 Global classical solutions for small initial data. Proof of Theorem 1.2

As mentioned in the introduction, the result featured in Theorem 1.2 is a by-product of our previous analysis. Our main tools in the proof will on one hand be the fact that the assumed smallness conditions for the initial data, expressed in (1.24) and (1.25), allows for the choice of t0=0t_{0}=0 in Lemma 4.3, and on the other hand the uniqueness statement from Lemma 2.1.
